en: Preface to the Collected Commentary on the Southern Edition of the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra:
As for the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra, it is the testament of the Tathāgata’s final charge. It was accumulated over kalpas of vast time and remained long hidden without being spoken.

Through skillful means to harmonize the capacities of beings, it was revealed only when the time was ripe. Thus, it stands in contrast to the Small Vehicle and the provisional teachings, encompassing both the partial and the complete.

The full blossoming of the school’s tenets—the proclamations on the sudden and gradual, the partial and the perfect, and the beginning, middle, and end—this profound essence is the ultimate discourse delivered at the very last.
It is like the precious treasures within a storehouse finally bestowed at the moment of death, or the divine jewels of the ocean that perish only when the kalpa ends.

How great is the World-Honored One! His compassion is peerless; with diligent seeking and exhaustive effort, he equally rescues those submerged in the depths of suffering, waiting for the opportune moment throughout forty-nine days.

Throughout my years, my original aspiration has not yet been fully realized. On the fifteenth day of the second month, when I proclaimed my passing into extinction, I have completely poured forth my innermost thoughts.

Thus, even those outside the ten [vehicles] who take refuge, including the icchantikas, have attained awakening; insects, grasses, and trees have all received his grace; elephants, horses, snakes, and vipers have all been bathed in his benevolence.
Those at the stages of inner and outer ordinary beings have surpassed the merits of kalpas; gods and humans alike have realized the fruit of non-arising. He is able to—
When his affairs were concluded, he immediately entered *nirvāṇa*. Thereupon, the sun and moon lost their radiance, and the mountains and forests turned white.

The great earth shook violently, and birds and beasts wailed in grief. Both the ordinary and the holy lost their celestial protector; among sentient and insentient beings alike, who did not lament and yearn for him?
Thus we know that once this sutra was proclaimed, nothing remained to be left behind. It is ultimate and exhaustive; none other can surpass it.
Furthermore, the old translation in forty fascicles was rendered with clumsy diction and excessive verbiage. Zhiyan Lingyun revised it to achieve brevity of expression and directness of principle.

Regarding the classification of the school’s tenets, five, seven, or eight masters have offered their views; Guanding has examined them with great precision, preserving both their merits and defects. Consequently, I have again investigated the ultimate truth and annotated this *Mysterious Text* (*Xuanwen*).
Alas, due to the military chaos of the Chen and Sui dynasties, these commentaries failed to enter the canon. Thus, they were scattered in different directions, as if by an irresistible force.

In the Wu-Yue region, let alone the fact that [this scripture] has long been hidden within the canon such that scholars rarely glimpse it; in this degenerate age, people are entirely exhausted by the ultimate Way.
This has caused the Dharma-eye to become clouded and the Buddha-sun to sink into obscurity. Alas! How painful! It truly wounds my heart and soul.

Therefore, disregarding my own foolishness and mediocrity, I have ventured to imitate the ancients; desiring to synthesize this sutra, I have devoted myself to this task for many days, reflecting upon it again and again.
Having perused this work, I have gained a rough understanding of its essential purport; yet, alas, the meaning is profound and the text is deep.
Following the example of Guo Xiang, I have jumbled the preceding and succeeding sections, suffering much like one who loses his way and forgets the sheep.

Therefore, fearing not the sin of an icchantika and willingly accepting the transgression of slandering the Dharma, I have pared away the redundant and recorded only the essentials, valuing above all a thorough comprehension. Whether this brings sin or merit, I offer my repentance for both.

Now that the Northern Edition already contains four and a half chapters, it is said that the latter portion includes the *Cien* (Cunda) chapter and fully conveys the intent of Subhadra’s final physical existence.
Furthermore, it contains the *Yijiao* (Bequeathed Teaching), *Huanyuan* (Returning to the Source), *Pinbi* (Discriminating the Teachings), and *Kuo* (Broadening) chapters.

(Tánghéng) Not deeming my own virtue sufficient, I have ventured to attempt this integration. Should there be any errors or omissions, I repent before the compassion of the Triple Gem.
With these humble causes, I pray for the Sage Emperor’s blessings and longevity to extend for ten thousand years, and I beseech that all the common people may together realize Bodhi.

May I, in life after life, rely upon this as a Dharma-ship, vowing never to abandon it until I have ascended to the shore of Enlightenment. May I, in every generation, hold this as a precious mirror, until I have emerged from the world of suffering.
Mārajāla. May we protect one another for all time. May the parents of this present life and the parents of kalpas past awaken together to the Buddha-nature of the One Vehicle.
May those who have been enemies or kin throughout accumulated lifetimes, as well as all beings within the *dharmadhātu*, together maintain the six recollections.

By cultivating the five practices and firmly upholding the ten virtues, may they fulfill them completely until the realm of sentient beings is exhausted, before finally attaining *bodhi*. [Until] hell is... [not yet].
I vow not to attain Buddhahood until [this] emptiness [is realized].

and the assembly of other devotees have resolved to carve this one volume of the *Commentary on the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
We humbly pray that the members of this assembly, by virtue of this merit, may cause their parents from successive lifetimes to transcend [suffering] in every way.

Ascending, may all karmic enemies and kin throughout the kalpas equally attain liberation. May the sun of Great Nirvāṇa shatter the dark alleys of ignorance, and the celestial realm of secret meaning universally encompass the Dharma-realm.

Through the six recollections and three cultivations, may there be constant permeation and hearing from life to life; through the five practices and ten virtues, may there be accomplishment everywhere.
Together we shall realize perfect Bodhi and each receive the final entrustment. Thus begins the first of the three assemblies at the Dragon Flower Tree.

On the Mid-Autumn Festival of the Renyin year, Grand Master Zhan came from Kuaiji and visited me.
On the desk before me was the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra* from the Southern Canon. He asked, "From where did you obtain this, Layman? I replied, "I retrieved it from among some discarded books."

This was left behind from a previous life. The Master sighed deeply and said: "In the past, during the chaos between the Sui and Chen dynasties, the elder Guanding picked up scraps of paper used for window caulking and recorded this commentary.
He endured myriad hardships; his chief disciple, Zhanran, desired to synthesize it with the sutra but did not succeed.
It remained buried within the canon for nearly a thousand years, rarely seen by scholars. I shall now analyze and synthesize it."
Entering the text of the scripture: [The author] had made a vow but had not yet attained it. "If you, Layman Guo, would circulate this for me," [the author] replied, "Yes, yes.
Thirteen years later, in the first month of winter in the year of Yimao (1075), the Master came to our commandery and preached the Dharma at the East Pagoda of Fucheng.
On a day of leisure, they met by the banks of the Linshui River. The Master said, "My commentary on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is now complete," and he brought out the draft to show him.
Furthermore, he said: "For several days, I was nearly thwarted by the demon of illness. I wept before the Buddha day after day, vowing to prolong my remaining breaths so as to complete this vow.
Before long, the illness subsided. I then extensively invited calligraphers and, burning oil lamps to continue through the night, it was finally completed after several more months.
Will you not honor your previous promise, Layman? I replied: "The unfinished case of an ancient virtuous one has been entrusted to you; may you not begrudge your efforts."

Dedicating my body and life for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, I venture to fulfill my prior promise. Consequently, on the eighth day of the twelfth month, I assembled craftsmen and set the woodblocks in motion.

Fortunately, relying on the joyful assistance of like-minded companions, the work was completed. In the autumn of the Ding-si year, I have respectfully recorded these details of the origin and the dates.
Recorded by Shen Yuchang of Wutang on the first day of the first month of winter in the Ding-si year.
Qi’s original name was Qiyin. From childhood, he had known to revere the Triple Gem.

In the spring of the Ding-si year, he attended Grand Master Zhan’s lecture on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* at the East Pagoda of Fucheng, going there every day to listen. He subsequently took refuge in the Master and received his current dharma name.

Previously, the commentary for the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* assembly had been prepared for carving and distribution; however, the task was vast while the funds were meager, causing the Master great anxiety. Qi...
He was then moved by the thought of taking up the burden of his father’s unfinished tasks; unconsciously, he shed tears of sorrow. That evening, he had a dream:

he saw the Great Master entering the hall before which a large bathing basin had been set out. The Master’s body was smeared with mud; he emerged from the basin after bathing, and his head had grown a foot longer.

Zhiqi looked at his own feet, which were also covered in mud, and followed him in turn into the bath. He then awoke. Upon waking, he interpreted the omen according to the numerical divination system (*shushu*).
However, he said to himself with joy, "The dream I had last night was clear; its imagery portends *nirvāṇa*.
Since the Master is propagating the Great Dharma, it is fitting that his head should be several feet long. That Qi also washed his feet must be an omen of success to be realized in the future.
That evening was the fourth day of the fourth month. He then resolved to recruit sponsors on his behalf and obtained forty units from his disciple Zhang Xiankai.

Gold was provided, and those who assisted in succession did so with varying degrees of contribution. By proceeding with double the usual diligence, the work was completed at the end of the seventh month.

From the night of the dream until the completion of the construction, it took only one hundred and twenty days. Thus, this account is recorded to demonstrate that the circulation of the Dharma was not a matter of mere coincidence.
Regarding the names of the donors, it was initially decided that they need not be engraved, as the project was initiated by those of virtuous faith.
The hearts of dragons and devas perceive all clearly; however, fearing that those in the mundane world might be ignorant of cause and effect, I have recorded each item solicited by Qi in full detail.
When the Master was lecturing on the Lotus Sūtra at Haiyan, thieves stole two boxes belonging to his attendant.
During the recruitment process, many individuals were lost or failed to have their names recorded at the end of the register;

this was due solely to the protection of the Dharma-protecting deity Vajrapāṇi, and truly for no other reason. Later, several names were recovered through a piecemeal search, which are appended below.
